segments.t: Stunned by the Chef's announcement, Max asks what test he is talking about. A series of flashbacks reveals that Viktor Petrovich carefully staged Lyova's sudden vacation and Fedya's refusal to work in order to see how Max would handle running the kitchen in an emergency.
Let's walk back through the scene line by line.
'What test are you talking about?' Here the Russian phrasing highlights 'what' before landing on 'inspection'.
'What do you think?' Lyova anchors the line on 'and', while 'think' completes the thought. Chef Viktor answers right away.
'You signed the request form yourself.' The plural past ending '-li' on the verb for 'to sign' covers a group or the polite 'you'.
'Was I drunk when I signed it?' Spoken Russian keeps this brisk, leaning on 'I' and finishing on 'there was'.
'Well, then it does not count.' Notice how Russian expresses 'come on' and 'to be considered' with crisp inflection rather than helper words. Lyova answers right away.
'You should have warned me beforehand.' Lyova anchors the line on 'to warn', while 'there was' completes the thought.
'It is not my fault.' In Russian, the idea of 'and' flows naturally into 'guilty' without extra filler words.
'That you are drunk all the time.' Notice how Russian expresses 'what' and 'drunk' with crisp inflection rather than helper words. Chef Viktor answers right away.
'Quite an actor even without you.' In Russian, the idea of 'without' flows naturally into 'actor' without extra filler words.
'What happened in the evening?' Here the Russian phrasing highlights 'in the evening' before landing on 'there was'.
'I do not know anything.' Spoken Russian keeps this brisk, leaning on 'nothing' and finishing on 'know'. Lyova answers right away.
'I have plans.' The meaning hinges on 'by' working together with 'plans' in spoken Russian.
'Chef, everything is ready.' Notice how Russian expresses 'chef' and 'ready' with crisp inflection rather than helper words. Let's hear the full exchange one more time at natural speed.
